lawyer:
Naima Haider, with Ms Mubina Asaf Rahman, Advocates —For the Petitioners. 
Abul Kalam Azad, Advocate — For the Opposite Parties No.1-11.
parties:
Shamsul Alam and others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Muslehuddin @ Md Muslem and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule issued in an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure calls in question a judgment and decree dated 26 September, 1990 passed by learned Additional District Judge, Cox's Bazar in Other Appeal No.94 of 1986 reversing those dated 17 May, 1986 passed by learned Upazila Munsif, Ukhiya, Cox's Bazar, in Other Suit No.26 of 1984 awarding decree in favour of the plaintiff side.

2. The Rule has been obtained by the petitioners raising the question as to whether the judgment of the lower appellate Court reversing the judgment of the trial Court was well founded on law.

3. For the purpose of answering to the said question posed, the relevant facts are stated briefly, which are as follows:

The predecessor of the opposite party Nos. 1-11 Eshaque Ahmed Sikder as sole plaintiff on 30-9-1980, instituted a suit being Other Suit No.471 of 1980 in the Court of Munsif, Cox's Bazar for declaration of title and confirmation of possession over 0.29 acre of land described in the schedule to the plaint. The schedule land is hereinafter referred to as the suit land. The suit was, thereafter, transferred to the Court of Upazila Munsif, Ukhiya and re-numbered there as Other Suit No.26 of 1984.

4. Sur Ali, Muklesh, Musa Ali and their mother, Ali Bibi were the owners of the suit land and the record of right was prepared in their names. The plaintiff purchased the said land by way of two sale deeds dated 31-1-1946 and 18-5-1952 from the heirs of the said recorded owners. RS record was prepared in the name of Sur Ali and other owners. The plaintiff had no knowledge of the wrong record in the name of Sur Ali and others, The MRR Khatian had been also prepared in the name of Sur Ali and others and the said record is absolutely wrong. The suit land was sold in auction for arrears of rent due to the Government in a certificate case of the year 1960 and was purchased by the defendants. The certificate case was stated making the recorded owners Sur Ali and others as certificate debtors. The certificate proceeding is collusive, illegal, void and without jurisdiction. The certificate sale was not acted upon and the auction purchaser did not acquire any right, title and possession on the suit land and the right, title and interest of the plaintiff has not been affected by the auctions sale. The defendants, though purchased the suit land from the auction purchaser, got no title and possession there and the suit land is possessed by the plaintiff. The cause of the suit arose on 8th Aswin, 1387 BS when the defendants, in the event of plaintiff''s dispossession over the suit or a portion of the suit land by the defendants.

6. The sole plaintiff having been dead, his heirs were substituted in his place as plaintiffs in the suit who are opposite party Nos. 1-11 in the Rule.

7. The defendant Nos. 5-7 entered appearance in the suit and contested the same by filing written statement traversing all the material allegations made in the plaint. It is the case of the defendant that the suit land originally belonged to Sur Ali and others and RS Khatian was prepared in their names. On the acquisition of rent receiving interest by the Government, they became tenants under the Government and MRR Khatian was correctly prepared in their names. For arrear of rents due to the Government with respect to the suit land, Certificate Case No.7402 of 1959-60 was started against the recorded owners of MRR Khatian and the land was put to auction and one Mir Ahmed auction purchased the suit land and got actual physical possession on 7-11-1962 through a Miscellaneous Case No. 53 of 1962-63 and possessed the land on payment of rents to the Government. The auction purchase Mir Ahmed transferred the auction purchased land to one Khatun and the said Khatun also exercised acts of possession over the suit land and on her death, the same was inherited by the defendant Nos. 1-4 and Mohammad Hussain, Shafiqur Rahman and Azizur Rahman. Mohammad Hussain, Shafiqur Rahman and Azizur Rahman transferred land of their share in favour of defendant Nos. 5-7 by four registered sale deeds on different dates the defendants encircled their purchased land with boundaries made a Kuria on some portion of the land and exercised acts of possession over the rest land. The defendant Nos. 1-4 sold land of their share to one Noorjahan.

8. Further case of the defendants is that, the alleged kabala deeds of the plaintiffs got no legal existence and those are forged, created and collusive deeds. The plaintiff, on the basis of those forged kabala deeds, did never exercise any act of possession on the suit land. MRR Khatian had been prepared 22 years back but the plaintiff did never make any attempt to have the MRR Khatian corrected. The plaintiff did not put forward any claim within twelve (12) years of the date of auction purchase and also of taking of the delivery of possession on the auction purchased land by the auction purchaser and the plaintiff claim and the suit stood barred by limitation. The plaintiff got no cause of action to file the suit against the defendants. The suit as framed is also not maintainable.

9. On these pleadings, the parties fought out the suit.

10. The learned trial Judge held that it had been proved that Mir Ahmed purchased the land in auction and went into possession by filing Miscellaneous Case No. 53 of 1962-63 and after that the defendants acquired title and possession over the suit land by virtue of sale deeds. The trial Judge further held that it had been proved that by the sale deeds, Exhibit-3 and 4, the plaintiffs did not get into possession over the suit land and the suit land by and the said deeds were not acted upon and by the auction sale, the title of the plaintiffs, if any, had been extinguished. The trial Judge held, further, that all the PWs admitted that the defendants possessed some portion of the suit land by encircling the same with fencing and that had been also proved by Exhibit-5, the Report of the Advocate Commissioner and some PWs admitted that the defendants were in possession over the entire suit land and the defendants grew ''pelong dal'' there. The trial judge came to the finding that MRR Khatian had been prepared long after the plaintiff obtained sale deeds but no attempt had been made by him to have the MRR Khatian, corrected. The trial judge found, further, that it was natural that the recorded owners of the suit land would be the certificate debtors. The trial judge found that the plaintiffs though were required to file suit for setting the sale did not do that. The trial judge, ultimately, expressed the view that the suit as framed was not maintainable and the same was barred by limitation. With the above findings, the trial judge negative the claim of the plaintiffs and dismissed the suit.

11. The plaintiffs, being aggrieved by the decision of the trial judge, carried an appeal to the Court of learned District Judge, Cox''s Bazar. The learned Additional District Judge heard the appeal set aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court and decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs.

12. The appellate Court in reversing the decision of the trial Court held that trial Court unnecessarily emphasized the question of possession of the suit land and the question of possession was not the subject matter of the suit but at the same time held that since the suit was for recovery of khas possession, the question of dispossession is significant. The appellate Court further held that the exhibits-3 and 4, the sale deeds of the year 1946 and 1952, were self-exhibited documents and those documents strengthen the claim of the plaintiffs. The appellate Court next found that the sale deeds in favour of Fatema Khatun had not been produced in the Court and thus the acquisition of title over the suit land by Fatema Khatun had not been proved. The appellate Court again found that the plaintiffs went into possession after purchase and since the plaintiffs were in possession, there was no question on the part of Mir Ahmed to go into possession over the suit land in the year 1962. The appellate Court further held that the certificate case was required to be filed against the persons who were in possession of the land and not those whose name had been recorded in the record of right and by the auction purchase no right accrued to the auction purchaser, Mir Ahmed. The appellate Court further held that the defendants, after creating some deeds, dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land and the suit had been filed within the period of dispossession.

13. The defendants being aggrieved by the aforesaid decision of learned Additional District Judge moved this Court in an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

14. Ms Naima Haider, learned Advocate appearing in support of the Rule, directed her arguments in assailing the impugned judgment of the lower appellate Court and contended that the lower appellate Court having not at all adverted to the reasoned decision on which the trial Court''s judgment rested and the impugned judgment having not been a proper judgment of reversal, the same cannot be sustained in law.

15. Ms Naima Haider contended, first, the plaintiff-opposite-parties did not seek any relief with respect to the auction sale held in the certificate proceeding and in the event of subsistency of the auction sale, plaintiff-petitioners were not at all entitled to have any declaration of title and confirmation of possession or in the alternative of recovery of khas possession over the suit land and the suit, thus, was at all maintainable.

16. The next contention advanced on behalf of the defendant-petitioners is that, the lower appellate Court did not find at what point of time the alleged dispossession of the plaintiffs occurred and whether the plaintiff's suit was instituted within 12 years of the date of dispossession as alleged by the plaintiffs.

17. The next argument addressed from the side of the petitioners is that the lower appellate Court committed a substantial error of law in finding that the question of possession was not material in the suit and that the learned trial Court was wrong in over emphasizing the question of possession in as much as the suit having been for declaration of title with confirmation of possession or recovery of khas possession, the question of possession was very much material specially when the trial Court categorically held that the kabalas in favour of the plaintiffs were never acted upon and the findings and reasons of the trial Court were neither adverted to nor reversed by the lower appellate Court.

18. Mr Abdul Kalam Azad, learned Advocate representing the plaintiff-opposite parties, on the other hand, submitted that the findings of the trial Court were not based on evidence and materials on record but the findings of the lower appellate Court were based on proper assessment and consideration of the evidences and other materials on record and, as such, the impugned judgment cannot be said as not being, a proper judgment of reversal. It is the further contention of the learned Advocate that the plaintiffs were required to be made parties in the certificate case as certificate debtors and in the absence of the plaintiffs as certificate debtors in the certificate case, the same could not be binding upon them.

19. It is further canvassed on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite parties that the sale deed of Fatema Khatun from the auction purchaser Mir Ahmed has not been filed in the Court by the defendants and the title deeds of the defendants cannot be considered unless the title deed of their vendor, Fatema Khatun is produced before the Court.

20. In the wake of rival contentions raised from both the sides, let me now consider the soundness of the contentions raised.

21. The mandate of law is that the lower appellate Court being the last and final Court of fact, is required to discuss and consider the evidences of the parties and other materials on record and in reversing any judgment of the trial Court, it is required to advert to the findings and decisions on which the trial Court''s judgment rested. Keeping in view of this mandate of law, let me see whether the judgment of the lower appellate Court reversing the decision of the trial Court can be sustained in law or not.

<u>22. Plaintiff in paragraph No. 4 and 5 of the plaint pleaded that the defendants expressed that the suit land i.e., the land of RS Khatian, for arrears of rents, was sold in auction in 1960 and they purchased the land from the auction purchaser and in the event of disclosure of any Bainama (sale certificate) and Dakhalnama (Writ of delivery of possession), those will be regarded as illegal, ineffective and baseless and the said auction sale was not acted upon and the auction purchaser and his successors did not acquire any title. PW 1 in his evidence stated that the whole auction matter is absolutely false and the auction sale was not acted upon and the auction purchaser did not exercise any acts of possession over the auction purchased land. The defendant-petitioners in the written statement clearly stated that the suit land, for arrears of rents was put to auction in a Certificate Case No. 7402 of 1959-60 and one Mr Ahmed auction purchased the land and got actual physical possession on 7-11-1962 through Miscellaneous Case No. 53 of 1962-63 and possessed the land on payment of rents to the Government. It was further pleaded that the auction purchaser Mir Ahmed transferred auction purchased land to one Fatema Khatun and on the death of Fatema Khatun, her heirs being the owners of the land, transferred their share to the defendant Nos.5-7 and Noorjahan Evidence had been also led in support of the auction sale and possession of the defendants following auction purchase. Exhibit-Ka is the writ of delivery of possession in favour of the auction purchaser Mr Ahmed on 7-11-1972 in Miscellaneous Case No. 53 of 1962-63. The trial Court on consideration of the evidences and materials on record came to the finding that it has been proved that suit land was auction sold for arrear of rent due to the Government and it was the responsibility of the plaintiffs to file suit seeking relief against the auction sale which the plaintiffs did not do so. On perusal of the impugned judgment, it does not appear that the appellate Court below has adverted to this most important aspect of the case. It appears that the lower appellate Court has not addressed itself to the clear finding arrived at by the trial Court that it was the responsibility of the plaintiffs to seek relief against the auction sale. The appellate Court did not come to any positive finding whether the plaintiffs were required to seek relief against the auction sale. The Power appellate Court simply found that the decisions arrived at by the trial Court to the effect that the claim of the plaintiffs could not be eatertainable as because plaintiffs, on getting knowledge of the auction purchase, did not file any suit against the auction purchase, were not proper but it did not meet the positive finding arrived at by the trial Court that it was the responsibility of the plaintiffs to file suit against the auction sale.</u>

<u>23. It had earlier been pointed out that plaintiffs did not seek any relief against the auction sale. The plaintiff also did not seek any relief with respect to the kabala deeds of the defendants dated 124-1977, 21-6-1997, 28-9-1978 and 22-12-1981. No issues were framed on auction sale and the sale deeds of the defendants.</u>

Issues framed in the suit were as follows:

১। অত্র মোকাদ্দমা বর্তমান আকারে সচল কি না?

২। অত্র মোকদ্দমা তামাদিতে বারিত কি না?

৩। অত্র মোকদ্দমা পক্ষ দোষে দুষ্ট কি না?

৪। মামলাটির উচিৎ মূল্যায়নে যথার্থ কোর্ট ফি আদায় করা হইয়াছে কি না?

৫। নালিশী জমিতে বাদীদের কথিত মতে স্বত্ব দখল আছে কি না?

৬। বাদীগণ তাহাদের প্রার্থীত মতে অত্র মামলায় ডিক্রি পাইতে পারে কি না?

The PW 1 who gave evidence for himself and also on behalf of other plaintiffs, in evidence sought decree of declaration of Rayati right and confirmation of possession over the suit land.

Relief sought for is extracted below:

প্রার্থনা নালিশী তফছিলের জমিতে বাদীদের খরিদা রায়তী স্বত্ব সাব্যস্তে দখল স্থিরতরের ডিক্রি চাই।

So, it is manifestly clear that plaintiff side, neither in the plaint nor in the evidence sought the relief against the auction sale and the sale deeds of the defendants with respect to the suit land but the lower appellate Court in the impugned judgment granted decree declaring the auction purchase in the name of Mir Ahmed and the sale deeds in the names of the defendants with respect to the suit land illegal. The lower appellate Court, thus, appeared to have traveled beyond the pleadings and evidences of the parties and, thus, committed substantial error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning a failure of justice.

24. Admittedly, Revisional Settlement (RS) Khatian had been prepared in the name of Sur Ali and others. The original plaintiff Eshaque Ahmed Sikder claimed to have purchased the suit land by way of two sale deeds registered on 5-2-1946 and 21-8-1952. Exhibits 3 and 4. MRR Khatian had been prepared long after the date of registration of the sale deeds of the plaintiffs. In the MRR Khatian, the name of the original plaintiff Eshaque Ahmed Sikder had not been recorded, rather the names of the RS recorded owners Sur Ali and others had been recorded in the Said MRR Khatian. The original plaintiff Eshaque Ahmed Sikder did not take any step to have the MRR Khatian corrected in his name. The trial Court found that the plaintiff did not make any attempt to have the record of right corrected in his name. The lower appellate Court also found that immediately after purchase, the plaintiff was required to get his name mutated in the connected record of right and due to non-recording of his name in the record of right, the certificate proceeding had been started. The certificate case had been started showing the recorded owners of the MRR Khatian as certificate debtors. The certificate officer was not supposed to know whether there had been any subsequent transfer from the recorded owners and whether the transferee was in possession on the suit land. So, it is natural that only those persons whose name had been recorded in the Khatian would be made parties i.e., certificate debtors in the certificate proceeding. The trial Court appears to have duly considered this aspect of the matter but the lower appellate Court misdirected itself in its approach on this aspect of the matter and the observation made by the lower appellate Court does not appear to be a proper and sound observation.

25. It is worth noting here that the plaintiff side, though, appears to have claimed title over the suit land since purchase in the year 1946 and 1952, did not file any rent receipt showing payment of rent either to the Superior Landlords or to the Government Acquired Estate. The plaintiff produced seven (7) rent receipts showing payment of rents to the Government for the suit land, Exhibit-series. Exhibit 2(Chha) is a rent receipt dated 25-8-1977 which is prior to the institution of the suit but all other rent receipts are of the year 1980, 1981, 1982, 1983, 1984 and 1985, after the institution of the suit. The suit is filed on 30-9-1980. The trial Court held that the plaintiff, even if, acquired title over the suit land on the basis of sale deeds Exhibits-3 and 4, but, he having defaulted in payment of rent, the suit land was put to auction and Mir Ahmed auction purchased the land and got possession thereon. This finding arrived at by the trial Court was not met by the lower appellate Court.

26. Let me now turn back to the vital question, which is, whether the plaintiff side was entitled to get a decree of recovery of khas possession and also, whether the suit was barred by limitation.

27. The trial Court found that plaintiff side got no right, title and possession over the suit land and the auction purchaser, Mir Ahmed after getting actual physical possession over the land, got into possession and from him, the subsequent transferees including the defendants exercised acts of possession over the suit land. The trial Court, also, found that plaintiffs were in clear knowledge of the auction sale since the year 1962 and the suit was barred by limitation. The lower appellate Court found that the defendants after creating some deeds with respect to the suit land dispossessed the plaintiff from the said land and established their possession. The lower appellate Court, also, found that the suit had been filed within the prescribed period of dispossession and also within the stipulated period of the knowledge of the auction sale.

28. In the plaint the plaintiff, asserting possession on the suit land, prayed for declaration of title and confirmation of possession thereon. Relief ''Ka'' (T) is as follows:

(ক) নিম্ন তফছিলের জমিতে বাদীর খরিদ, কোর্কা, হাল রায়তী স্বত্ব সাব্যস্তে দখল স্থিরতরের ডিক্রি দেওয়ার।

The alternative relief of recovery of khas possession over the land from which the plaintiff would be dispossessed was sought, subsequently, by way of amendment, as pointed out earlier. Amended portion is extracted below:

বিকল্পে ইতি মধ্যে বিবাদীগণ বাদীকে নালিশী জমি কিংবা নালিশী জমিতে বাদীর রায়তী স্বত্ব সাব্যস্তে বিবাদীর অন্যায় যবর দখল উচ্ছেদে বাদীর বাস দখল দেওয়ার ডিক্রি হয়।

<u>29. From the above, it appears that plaintiff''s suit was for possession and subsequent dispossession and the case was squarely covered by Article 142 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act. Now I am to refer to the relevant oral evidences on record to decide the factum of possession of the plaintiff and the defendants over the suit land. Plaintiff 1(ka) as PW 1 gave evidence for himself and for all the plaintiffs. He was aged about 30 years on 5-3-1986 when the evidence was recorded. This PW 1 stated that he did not file any case for setting aside the auction sale. He further stated that the rent receipts filed in the Court were subsequent to the filing of the suit. PW1 further gave evidence that defendant Nos. 5-7 forcible entered into the suit land and were in possession over some portion of the suit land. Again, he stated that on his prayer dated 6-5-1981, Advocate Commissioner was appointed and Advocate Commissioner reported that defendants were in possession over some portion of the land. PW1 did not state the date of dispossession from the suit land. PW 2 was aged about 35 years. In his evidence he stated that the defendants forcibly took over possession over 6/7 karas of land 4/5 years back. He could not say the Khatian and plot number of the suit land. This witness, further, stated that the defendants possessed land by erecting fencing. This witness further stated that he could not say on which date the defendants dispossessed the plaintiff. PW 3 gave evidence that the defendants, 4/5 years back, forcibly possessed about 8 karas of land. This witness again stated that the defendants erected house over the suit land 8/10 years back. PW 4 testified that 2-4 years back, the defendants forcibly possessed the entire suit land. PW 5 testified that the defendants, 3-4 years back, forcibly possessed some land. PW 6 testified that the defendants forcibly possessed 7/8 karas of land out of the suit land. PW 7, the learned Advocate Commissioner, gave evidence that he found a 'Kuria' over the suit land.</u>

<u>30. On the other hand, defendant No. 5 as DW 1, gave testimony that the auction purchaser, Mir Ahmed got into possession over the auction purchased land through the process of law in Miscellaneous Case No. 53 of 1962 and he exercised acts of possession over the suit land. He gave further testimony that auction purchaser, Mir Ahmed sold the suit land to one Fatema Khatun and on the death of Fatema Khatun her heirs transferred the suit land to the defendant Nos. 5-7 and to other persons. He stated that the suit land is under their possession and the suit land is surrounded by fencing. He further stated that plaintiff side got no title and possession over any portion of the suit land. The evidence of DW 1 was corroborated by other DWs DW 4 Ahmed, the auction purchaser, gave evidence that on the basis of auction sale, he possessed the suit land and after him, Fatema Khatun, on the basis of a sale deed from him, possessed the land and on the death of Fatema Khatun, the defendant No. 5 possessed the suit land on the basis of sale deeds from the heirs of Fatema Khatun. DW 4 further testified that the process server by beating of drum inducted him in physical possession on the auction purchased land. This witness further stated that he transferred the auction purchased land to Fatema Khatun by way of a sale deed.</u>

<u>31. On an analysis of the evidence of the PWs it become evidently clear that, though, the plaintiffs pleaded possession over the suit land on the date of the institution of the suit, they were out of possession on the suit land, at least, with respect to some portion of the land, PW 4 admitted the possession of the defendants over the entire suit land. The evidences of other PWs on the question of dispossession from the suit land by the defendant suffer from contradictions and inconsistencies. Some PWs gave evidence that dispossession took place 2-4 years back whereas some PWs testified that dispossession took place 7-8 years back i.e., prior to the institution of the suit. It is significant to note here that plaintiff''s exclusive possession over the suit land since the year 1946 i.e. since the execution and registration of the first sale deed till the institution of the suit could not also be proved by any aged reliable witness. On the other hand, the possession of the auction purchaser and after him, the possession of Fatema Khatun and thereafter of the defendants over the suit land since the taking of the actual delivery of possession 7-11-1962, has been substantiated by legal evidences, Exhibit-'Kha' is the right of delivery of possession evidence in handing over of the possession of the suit land by the Process Server to the auction purchaser, Mir Ahmed and the legal effect of this Exhibit-Kha cannot be overlooked. It had been earlier pointed out that except one rent receipt, Exhibit 2(Chha), all other rent receipts were subsequent to the date of the institution of the suit. The defendant also filed a rent receipt dated 19-3-1980 showing payment of rent for the year 1385-1386 BS and this rent receipt is prior to the institution of the suit.</u>

<u>32. In RS Khatian No. 967 corresponding to MRR Khatian No. 9029, the plot No. being 4021, total land is 0.29 acres. Exhibit 3 is a Kabala deed dated 5-2-1946 executed by Musa Ali, Moklesur Rahman sons of Waziuddin, Mokbul Ali and Alimuddin sons of Sur Ali in favour of plaintiff Eshaque Ahmed transferring total 0.29 acre of land from the said plot and Khatian. Exhibit-4 is the Kabala deed dated 21-8-1952 registered by Suya Bibi and Anabibi other owners of the land, in favour of the said Eshaque Ahmed transferring 0.08 acre of land from the said plot Khatian No. Thus, the total land transferred came to 0.37 acres of land but there were only 0.29 acres of land in the said plot and Khatian. On scrutiny of the two Kabala deeds, Exhibit 3 and 4 it transpires that Exhibit-3 is only one page Kabala deed and Exhibit-4 is only one and a half page Kabala deed. MRR Khatian has been prepared long after the sale deeds of the plaintiffs and admittedly, the plaintiff did not make any step to have the MRR Khatian corrected. The trial Court, on a consideration of the two ''deeds Exhibits-3 and 4, the MRR Khatian, legal evidences and other materials on record came to the decision that the plaintiff, as a matter of fact, did not get into possession over the suit land and the said two sale deeds were not acted upon and the suit, having not been filed within the period of limitation prescribed by law, the same stood barred by limitation. The lower appellate Court does not appear to have reversed the said findings of the trial Court property. The appellate Court in a sweeping way without considering the legal evidences and other materials on record found that the cause of action had been proved and the suit had been filed within the period of dispossession. It needs be mentioned here that the trial Court on a proper discussion of the oral evidences of both the PWs and DWs came to a decision and dismissed the suit. It is surprising that the lower appellate Court in reversing the decision of the trial Court did not discuss the oral evidences of PWs and DWs which it was required to do being the last and final Court of fact. The appellate Court simply stated that the PW 1 admitted that the defendants prior to the institution of the suit forcibly possessed some portion of the suit land. The lower appellate Court was required to find on which date the plaintiff was dispossessed from the suit land and whether the suit was filed within 12 years from the date of dispossession to get a decree for recovery of Khas possession. My considered view is this that the question of limitation had not been properly treated by the lower appellate Court.</u>

<u>33. The lower appellate Court granted the relief of recovery of Khas possession over the entire suit land, although, the plaintiff did not seek the relief of recovery of Khas possession over the entire suit land. Rather, from the amendment, it transpires that recovery of khas possession was sought in a portion from where the act of dispossession would occur but curiously, it is pointed out that the area of the specific portion from where the alleged dispossession occurred, had not been stated in the amendment. So, awarding a decree of recovery of Khas possession with respect to the entire suit land, not sought for by the plaintiff, suffers from a gross illegality and also legal infirmity.</u>

34. The lower appellate Court found that the sale deed executed and registered by auction purchaser Mir Ahmed in favour of Fatema Khatun had not been submitted in the Court and the acquisition of title and possession over the suit land by Fatema Khatun as stated by the defendant, had not been proved. This finding of the lower appellate Court got no basis and the same, also, suffers from a gross error. On perusal of the record, it is found that the kabala deed executed registered on 5-1-1965 by the auction purchaser Mir Ahmed in favour of Fatema Khatun had been filed in the Court under regular Firisti on 21-4-1986 and the original Kabala deed is in the record. The finding arrived at by the lower appellate Court as to the non-production of the kabala deed of Fatema Khatun in the Court is the result of non-application of mind of the said Court. In this context, it is mentioned here that Mir Ahmed, the auction purchaser as DW 4 gave evidence that he transferred the land in favour of Fatema Khatun and on her death, her heirs transferred the suit land in favour of the defendant Nos. 5-7 and other persons.

35. The lower appellate Court at one time came to the finding that it was not the principal subject matter who possessed the suit land presently and at the same time found that since the suit was for decree of Khas possession, the act of dispossession was a matter of vital importance. The lower appellate Court found that it was to be decided on whom lawful title vested but found fault with the trial Court in making remarks that the lower Court unnecessarily gave importance on the factum of possession over the suit land and at the same time found that it could not be denied that the question of possession would be the decisive factor in determining the title. The findings of the lower appellate Court suffer from patent inconsistencies.

<u>36. Admittedly, MRR Khatian had been prepared long after the alleged kabala deeds of the plaintiffs and MRR Khatian stands in the name of the original owners Sur Ali and others. The MRR Khatian got a presumption of possession, at least, at the time when the same had been prepared and the correctness of the presumption of possession did not appear to have been rebutted by the plaintiff's side.</u>

37. It may be profitably pointed that the finding arrived at by the lower appellate Court that at the time of purchase of the suit land by the plaintiff, there had been no other claimant for the suit land and, as such, there could not be and believable ground for not going into possession over the suit land by the plaintiff any it had been proved that the title and possession of the suit land vested with the plaintiff since their purchase and the defendants created some deeds with respect to the suit land and by that it had been proved that at the relevant time after creating the said deeds, the defendant dispossessed the plaintiff from the suit land and established their possession there are not borne out from the evidences and materials on record. The appellate Court did not give any reasons in coming to those findings and the findings are vitiated by error of law.

38. It is well known that the finding of fact arrived at by the appellate Court, being the last and final Court of fact, shall not be disturbed by the High Court but it is equally, also, well known that the finding of fact, to attain immunity from attack must be based on evidences and materials on record. If a finding is not based on evidence or if it is based on inadequacy of evidence, then interference is justified. The finding of fact not supported by any cogent reason is not finding in the eye of law. It has already been pointed out that the lower appellate Court as the last and final Court of fact, though required to discuss the evidences of the witnesses of both the parties, did not discuss the evidences of the witnesses of both the parties and, thus, committed an error. It has also been noticed that the findings of the lower appellate Court suffered from patent inconsistencies and those were vitiated by grave error of law. It has, also, been noted that the findings were not justified from the evidences and materials on record and the impugned judgment suffered from gross illegality and legal infirmity and the same could not be said to be a proper judgment of reversal. And by all these errors and illegalities, the ultimate decision in the appeal has been seriously affected. My considered view is that since the decisions arrived at by the lower appellate Court had been vitiated by error of law, those cannot claim immunity from being attacked in the exercise of jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Interference is, therefore, called for.

39. In view of the discussions made herein above, I find that the Rule got substance and the same, thus, succeeds.

40. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The impugned judgment and decree dated 26-9-1990 passed in other Appeal No.94 of 1986 of the Court of Additional District Judge, Cox's Bazar is set aside and the judgment and decree passed in other Suit No. 26 of 1984 passed by Upazila Munsif, Ukhiya, Cox's Bazar is restored.

41. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, I direct the parties to bear their respective costs.

LCR be sent down immediately.

End.
